tiles.title: DataFrames, Series, and Reading Data
tiles.summary: Learn the two core pandas data structures — Series and DataFrame — and how to load tabular data from CSV and Excel files into a DataFrame.

steps.title: Two building blocks: Series and DataFrame
steps.lede: Every pandas table is built from just two structures. Understanding them makes every later operation predictable.

blocks.text: A pandas **Series** is a one-dimensional labeled array that can hold data of any type. Its axis labels are collectively called the **index**. Think of it as a single column of a spreadsheet: each cell has a value, and each row has a label on the left.

A Series can be built from a Python list, a dict, or a scalar. `pd.Series([18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80])` — SwiftDrop delivery times — gets index labels 0 through 6 by default. `pd.Series({"Lagos": 18, "Abuja": 20, "Kano": 22})` uses the dict keys as the index instead.

A pandas **DataFrame** is a two-dimensional labeled data structure whose columns can hold different types. It can be thought of as a dict of Series objects that all share the same index — one Series per column, all aligned row-by-row.

blocks.title: A DataFrame is a collection of Series sharing one index
blocks.alt_text: A DataFrame shown as three columns side by side — order_id, city, delivery_time_minutes — each highlighted as a Series, all sharing the same index (0, 1, 2) on the left.

blocks.text: Pass a dict of equal-length lists to `pd.DataFrame()` and each key becomes a column name: `pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1001, 1002, 1003], "city": ["Lagos", "Abuja", "Kano"], "delivery_time_minutes": [18, 20, 22]})` produces a three-column, three-row orders table.

A DataFrame behaves like a dict of like-indexed Series. `orders['city']` returns the city column as a Series. `orders['courier'] = ['Ada', 'Bayo', 'Chidi']` adds a new column — the same bracket syntax you use to read or write a dict entry.

steps.title: Loading CSV and Excel files into a DataFrame
steps.lede: Delivery records often arrive as CSV exports or Excel workbooks. Two pandas functions cover both.

blocks.text: Before pandas can work with your delivery records, you read the file into a DataFrame. `pd.read_csv("orders.csv")` is the main function for reading a delimited text file — such as a CSV — into a DataFrame. `pd.read_excel("orders.xlsx", sheet_name="January")` reads an Excel workbook instead.

`read_csv()` takes the file path (or URL) as its first argument. `read_excel()` additionally takes `sheet_name` to choose which sheet to load — that is why the Excel call names `"January"` but the CSV call does not need to. `read_csv()` also accepts `sep` to change the field delimiter: `pd.read_csv("orders.csv", sep=";")` handles a semicolon-delimited export correctly.

before.code:
# orders.csv — plain text on disk
order_id,city,delivery_time_minutes
1001,Lagos,18
1002,Abuja,20
1003,Kano,22

# Read it into a DataFrame
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")

steps.title: Two ways to build a DataFrame from Python data
steps.lede: Not every DataFrame starts life as a file. When delivery data already exists as Python objects, you can build the table directly.

blocks.text: Pass a **dict of equal-length lists** to `pd.DataFrame()` and each key becomes a column name; each list becomes that column's values. With no index argument the result uses a default range index: `orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1001, 1002, 1003], "city": ["Lagos", "Abuja", "Kano"]})`.

Alternatively, pass a **list of dicts** where each dict becomes one row and the dict keys become column names: `orders = pd.DataFrame([{"order_id": 1001, "city": "Lagos"}, {"order_id": 1002, "city": "Abuja"}])`. Both routes produce the same kind of table — pick whichever shape your data is already in.

tiles.title: Selecting and Filtering Data
tiles.summary: Use .loc and .iloc to select rows and columns by label or position, and apply boolean filters — single conditions or combined with & | ~ — to keep only the rows you need.

steps.title: Two accessors: .loc for labels, .iloc for positions
steps.lede: Pandas gives two different accessors depending on whether you want to address rows by their labels or by their integer positions.

blocks.text: `.loc` selects data **by label** — row index labels and column names. `.iloc` selects data **by integer position**, from 0 to length−1 of the axis. Both accept a row selector and a column selector separated by a comma: `df.loc[rows, cols]`. A colon (`:`) or omitting an axis means 'all of that axis'.

`orders.loc[2:4, "city"]` selects the `city` column for the rows **labeled** 2 through 4 — and because `.loc` uses label slicing, **both endpoints are included** in the result. So `orders.loc[2:4]` returns rows labeled 2, 3, and 4.

blocks.takeaway: .loc includes the stop label; .iloc excludes the stop position — double-check this boundary whenever a slice's last row matters.

steps.title: Selecting rows and columns with .loc and .iloc
steps.lede: Watch .loc and .iloc used on real tables to pick rows by label and by position.

steps.title: .iloc uses 0-based positions with an exclusive stop
steps.lede: iloc follows the same slicing rules as Python lists — the stop position is not included.

blocks.text: `orders.iloc[0:3, 0:2]` selects the first three rows (positions 0, 1, 2) and the first two columns (positions 0, 1) by pure position. The stop position 3 is **excluded**, following ordinary Python slicing rules. So `orders.iloc[0:3]` returns exactly three rows — not four.

steps.title: Filter rows with a True/False mask
steps.lede: Suppose you only want the delivery orders that took longer than 25 minutes — a boolean filter does exactly that.

blocks.text: Comparing a DataFrame column with a value — such as `orders['delivery_time_minutes'] > 25` — produces a **True/False Series** of the same length as the column. Passing that Series inside `orders[...]` keeps only the rows where the value is `True`.

When combining multiple conditions, each must be wrapped in parentheses and joined with `&` (and), `|` (or), or `~` (not). For example: `orders[(orders['city'] == 'Lagos') & (orders['delivery_time_minutes'] > 25)]`. Without the parentheses Python evaluates the comparison operators in the wrong order.

blocks.text: `.loc` selects by **label** and includes the stop label in a slice. `.iloc` selects by **integer position** and excludes the stop position, following Python slicing rules. Both accept `[rows, cols]` — a colon means 'all of that axis'.

A boolean filter is a same-length True/False Series you compute first, then pass to `df[...]` to keep only the matching rows. When combining conditions with `&`, `|`, or `~`, each condition must be in parentheses.

blocks.text: `orders.iloc[0:3]` returns rows at positions 0, 1, and 2 — **not** position 3. This is the same rule as Python list slicing: `my_list[0:3]` gives three items. Contrast with `.loc`: `orders.loc[0:3]` returns rows labeled 0, 1, 2, **and** 3 — the stop label is included. Always double-check which accessor you are using when the last row matters.

blocks.text: `orders['delivery_time_minutes'] > 25` produces a True/False Series the same length as the DataFrame. Passing it inside `orders[...]` keeps only the rows where the value is `True` — every row where the condition is `False` is dropped. The mask must be the same length as the DataFrame's index; pandas aligns them row by row.

remediation_steps.title: Parentheses are required when combining conditions
remediation_steps.lede: Each condition must be in its own parentheses before you join them with & or |.

blocks.text: When combining conditions, each must be grouped in parentheses: `orders[(orders['city'] == 'Lagos') & (orders['delivery_time_minutes'] > 25)]`. Without the parentheses, Python evaluates the comparison operators in the wrong order and raises a `ValueError`. The `&`, `|`, and `~` operators work element-wise on the boolean Series.

tiles.title: Sorting and Renaming
tiles.summary: Sort a DataFrame by one or more columns with sort_values, controlling ascending/descending order per column, and rename column and index labels with rename using a dict mapping.

steps.title: sort_values: sort by one or more columns
steps.lede: Reorder the rows of a DataFrame by the values in one or more columns.

blocks.text: `DataFrame.sort_values(by=...)` sorts rows using the values of the listed column(s). When `by` is a list, the first column sets the primary sort order and each later column breaks ties: `orders.sort_values(by=['city', 'delivery_time_minutes'])` sorts by city first, then by delivery time within each city.

The `ascending` parameter defaults to `True`. Pass a list of booleans matching the length of `by` to sort some columns ascending and others descending in the same call: `orders.sort_values(by=['city', 'delivery_time_minutes'], ascending=[True, False])` sorts cities alphabetically but delivery times from slowest to fastest within each city.

blocks.change_summary: Rows are reordered: city is the primary sort key; delivery_time_minutes breaks ties within each city.

steps.title: rename(): relabel columns and index entries with a dict
steps.lede: Clean up column names or row labels without rebuilding the DataFrame.

blocks.text: `rename()` relabels a DataFrame's axes using a dict mapping (or a function). Pass `columns=` to rename column labels: `orders.rename(columns={'delivery_time_minutes': 'delivery_min'})` renames that one column and leaves every other label unchanged.

A single `rename()` call can rename columns and index labels together by passing both `columns=` and `index=` at once: `orders.rename(columns={'city': 'destination_city'}, index={0: 'first_order'})` relabels one column and one row label in one call — any label not in the mapping is left as-is.

blocks.text: `sort_values(by=[...])` reorders rows by the listed columns. The first column is the primary sort key; later columns break ties. `ascending` defaults to `True` and can be a list of booleans to mix directions.

`rename(columns={...})` relabels column headers using a dict mapping; `rename(index={...})` relabels row index entries. Both can be combined in one call — any label not in the mapping is left unchanged.

tiles.title: Type Conversion and Datetime Handling
tiles.summary: Learn to convert column dtypes with astype and to work with datetime data using pd.to_datetime and the .dt accessor.

steps.title: Fixing column types with astype
steps.lede: When a CSV loads numbers as text, arithmetic fails. astype() converts a column to the right dtype in one call.

blocks.text: Suppose the SwiftDrop export loads `distance_km` as text — values like `"12.5"` instead of actual floats. Until the dtype is fixed, pandas treats the column as strings and arithmetic on it will fail.

The `astype()` method explicitly converts a column's values from one dtype to another, returning a copy by default. It raises an exception if the conversion is invalid — so `orders["distance_km"].astype(float)` converts text values to floats, but a row containing `"unknown"` would raise an error rather than silently guessing.
`astype()` can convert multiple columns at once by passing a dict: `orders.astype({"distance_km": float, "order_id": str})` converts two columns to two different target types in a single call.

before.code:
# distance_km loaded as object (text)
print(orders["distance_km"].dtype)  # object
print(orders["distance_km"].head())  # '4.2', '6.1', '5.5' ...

annotations.text: dtype is 'object' — pandas stores these as strings
Values look numeric but are text; arithmetic would fail

after.code:
orders["distance_km"] = orders["distance_km"].astype(float)
print(orders["distance_km"].dtype)  # float64
# Now arithmetic works: orders["distance_km"].mean()

annotations.text: astype(float) converts every text value to a real float
dtype is now float64 — arithmetic is possible

blocks.change_summary: distance_km column converted from object (text) to float64 using astype(float).

steps.title: Turning date text into real datetimes
steps.lede: A pickup_date column stored as text can't answer date questions. pd.to_datetime converts it, and .dt unlocks its components.

blocks.text: Suppose the SwiftDrop export records each order's `pickup_date` as plain text — `"2024-03-14"`. Before you can ask which month had the most deliveries, that text needs to become an actual datetime value.

`pd.to_datetime()` converts a Series of date-like strings into pandas datetime values, returning a Series with the same index: `orders["pickup_date"] = pd.to_datetime(orders["pickup_date"])` replaces the text column with genuine datetime values, one per order, in the same row positions.

Once a column has a datetime dtype, its `.dt` accessor exposes date component properties for each value: `orders["pickup_month"] = orders["pickup_date"].dt.month` pulls just the month number out of every pickup date at once.

before.code:
# pickup_date is object dtype (text)
print(orders["pickup_date"].dtype)   # object
print(orders["pickup_date"].head())  # '2024-03-14', '2024-03-14', '2024-03-15', ...

annotations.text: dtype is 'object' — dates stored as plain strings
Values look like dates but pandas can't do date arithmetic yet

after.code:
orders["pickup_date"] = pd.to_datetime(orders["pickup_date"])
orders["pickup_month"] = orders["pickup_date"].dt.month
print(orders["pickup_date"].dtype)   # datetime64[ns]
print(orders[["pickup_date", "pickup_month"]].head())

annotations.text: to_datetime converts text strings to real datetime values
.dt.month extracts the month number from each datetime
dtype is now datetime64[ns]

blocks.change_summary: pickup_date converted from object to datetime64 with pd.to_datetime; a new pickup_month column extracted via .dt.month.

steps.title: Type conversion and datetime handling — key takeaways
steps.lede: Two tools for fixing column types: astype for general conversions, to_datetime for dates.

blocks.text: `astype()` is the general-purpose dtype converter — pass a target type for one column or a dict for several at once. It raises an exception on invalid conversions rather than guessing. For date columns, `pd.to_datetime()` is the one-time conversion step; after that, `.dt` unlocks pulling out whatever date component the analysis needs.

blocks.text: `astype()` can convert a single column or multiple columns at once. Pass a dict mapping column names to target dtypes: `orders.astype({"distance_km": float, "order_id": str})` converts `distance_km` to float and `order_id` to string in one call — no need to call astype twice.

before.code:
# Two separate astype calls — works but verbose
orders["distance_km"] = orders["distance_km"].astype(float)
orders["order_id"] = orders["order_id"].astype(str)

annotations.text: Two separate calls — one per column

after.code:
# One astype call with a dict — converts both columns at once
orders = orders.astype({"distance_km": float, "order_id": str})

annotations.text: Dict maps each column name to its target dtype

blocks.change_summary: Two separate astype calls replaced by one dict-based call.

remediation_steps.title: Extracting date components with .dt
remediation_steps.lede: After converting a column to datetime, the .dt accessor exposes year, month, day, and more for every row at once.

blocks.text: Once a column has a datetime dtype, its `.dt` accessor exposes date/time component properties — such as `year`, `month`, and `day` — for each value: `orders["pickup_month"] = orders["pickup_date"].dt.month` pulls just the month number out of every pickup date at once. Without the `.dt` accessor, you cannot access these properties on a datetime Series.

before.code:
# pickup_date is still text — .dt is not available
# orders["pickup_date"].dt.month  # AttributeError

annotations.text: Text column has no .dt accessor — must convert first

after.code:
orders["pickup_date"] = pd.to_datetime(orders["pickup_date"])
orders["pickup_month"] = orders["pickup_date"].dt.month
orders["pickup_day"]   = orders["pickup_date"].dt.day

annotations.text: Convert once with to_datetime
.dt.month and .dt.day each extract one component for every row

blocks.change_summary: pickup_date converted to datetime; month and day extracted via .dt accessor.

tiles.title: Text Cleaning, Duplicates, and Missing Data
tiles.summary: Clean text columns with the .str accessor, remove duplicate rows with drop_duplicates, and handle missing values with isna, dropna, and fillna.

steps.title: Cleaning a text column with the .str accessor
steps.lede: Mixed-case and padded city names cause mismatches. The .str accessor applies string methods across an entire column at once.

blocks.text: Suppose the `city` column in a SwiftDrop export has `"Lagos"`, `" lagos"`, and `"LAGOS "` scattered across different rows — the same city, written three inconsistent ways. Grouping or filtering by city will miss rows until the values are standardised.

A Series' `.str` accessor lets you call ordinary string-processing methods — matching the names of Python's built-in string methods such as `lower`, `strip`, and `replace` — on every element of the Series at once: `orders["city"].str.strip().str.lower()` removes stray whitespace and lowercases every city value in one chained call, turning all three variants into the same `"lagos"`.

before.caption: city column before cleaning — mixed case and stray spaces

after.code:
orders["city"] = orders["city"].str.strip().str.lower()
print(orders["city"].unique())  # ['lagos', 'abuja', 'kano']

annotations.text: .str.strip() removes leading/trailing spaces; .str.lower() lowercases every value
All three variants now collapse to the same lowercase form

blocks.change_summary: city column cleaned: stray whitespace stripped and all values lowercased in one chained .str call.

steps.title: Lowercasing every value in a column at once
steps.lede: Watch a single .str.lower() call change every row in a column.

steps.title: Removing duplicate rows with drop_duplicates
steps.lede: A repeated order_id means the same order was logged twice. drop_duplicates removes the extra row, keeping the occurrence you choose.

blocks.text: Suppose order `#1003` appears twice in the SwiftDrop orders DataFrame, logged the same way both times. Any count or aggregation will be inflated until the duplicate is removed.

`duplicated()` returns a boolean vector indicating which rows are duplicates, and `drop_duplicates()` removes them; both accept a `subset` argument naming the columns used to identify a duplicated row: `orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"])` removes rows that repeat the same `order_id`.

By default, `drop_duplicates()` keeps the first occurrence of each duplicate set and drops the rest. Passing `keep='last'` keeps the last occurrence instead; `keep=False` drops every row that is part of a duplicate set: `orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"], keep="last")` would keep order `#1003`'s second logged row instead of its first.

before.caption: orders before deduplication — order_id 1003 appears twice

after.code:
orders_clean = orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"])
print(len(orders_clean))  # one row per order_id

annotations.text: subset=["order_id"] means two rows with the same order_id count as duplicates
Result has one row per unique order_id; first occurrence kept by default

blocks.change_summary: Duplicate order rows removed by drop_duplicates(subset=['order_id']); first occurrence kept.

steps.lede: Test your understanding of how drop_duplicates uses the subset argument.

steps.title: Detecting, dropping, and filling missing values
steps.lede: Blank cells in a DataFrame are missing values. isna detects them; dropna removes affected rows; fillna replaces them.

blocks.text: Suppose a handful of SwiftDrop orders never got a `delivery_time_minutes` recorded — those cells are just blank. Any mean or sum on that column will be wrong unless the gaps are handled first.
`isna()` (and its complement `notna()`) detects which values in a Series or DataFrame are missing: `orders["delivery_time_minutes"].isna()` returns `True` for every order missing that value.

`dropna()` removes rows that contain missing values; passing a `subset` of column labels restricts which columns are checked: `orders.dropna(subset=["delivery_time_minutes"])` removes only the orders missing that one column, ignoring gaps elsewhere.

`fillna()` replaces missing values with a specified value: `orders["delivery_time_minutes"].fillna(orders["delivery_time_minutes"].median())` replaces each missing delivery time with the column's median instead of dropping the order entirely.

before.caption: orders before handling missing values — some delivery_time_minutes are blank

after.code:
# Option A: drop rows missing delivery_time_minutes
orders_dropped = orders.dropna(subset=["delivery_time_minutes"])

# Option B: fill missing values with the column median
median_time = orders["delivery_time_minutes"].median()
orders["delivery_time_minutes"] = orders["delivery_time_minutes"].fillna(median_time)

annotations.text: dropna with subset removes only rows missing this column
fillna replaces each blank with the column's median value

blocks.change_summary: Missing delivery_time_minutes handled: either dropped with dropna(subset=...) or filled with the column median via fillna.

steps.title: Text cleaning, duplicates, and missing data — key takeaways
steps.lede: Three essential data-quality tools: .str for text, drop_duplicates for repeated rows, and isna/dropna/fillna for gaps.

blocks.text: Whatever string method you'd call on one piece of text, the `.str` accessor applies across an entire column at once. `drop_duplicates(subset=[...])` removes repeated rows by key column, keeping the first occurrence by default. Handling missing data means detecting it first with `isna()`, then deciding: drop the row if the missing field makes it unusable, or fill with a reasonable substitute such as the column's median.

remediation_steps.title: The .str accessor applies string methods to every row
remediation_steps.lede: Instead of looping row by row, the .str accessor vectorises any Python string method across the whole column.

blocks.text: A Series' `.str` accessor lets you call ordinary string-processing methods — matching the names of Python's built-in string methods such as `lower`, `strip`, and `replace` — on every element of the Series at once. `orders["city"].str.strip().str.lower()` removes stray whitespace and lowercases every city value in one chained call, turning `"Lagos"`, `" lagos"`, and `"LAGOS "` all into `"lagos"`.

annotations.text: Row-by-row loop — slow and verbose

after.code:
# With .str — one vectorised call
orders["city"] = orders["city"].str.strip().str.lower()

annotations.text: .str applies strip and lower to every element at once

blocks.change_summary: Row-by-row loop replaced by a single chained .str.strip().str.lower() call.

remediation_steps.title: Using subset to identify duplicate rows
remediation_steps.lede: drop_duplicates checks all columns by default. The subset argument limits the check to the columns that define a duplicate.

blocks.text: `duplicated()` returns a boolean vector indicating which rows are duplicates, and `drop_duplicates()` removes them; both accept a `subset` argument naming the columns used to identify a duplicated row. `orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"])` removes rows that repeat the same `order_id`, even if other columns differ slightly between the two rows.

before.code:
# Without subset — checks ALL columns; rows must be identical
orders.drop_duplicates()

annotations.text: Only removes rows where every column matches — misses partial duplicates

after.code:
# With subset — checks only order_id
orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"])

annotations.text: Removes any row whose order_id already appeared — correct for this case

blocks.change_summary: drop_duplicates called with subset=['order_id'] to catch rows with the same order ID regardless of other column differences.

remediation_steps.title: Drop or fill — choosing the right approach
remediation_steps.lede: dropna removes rows with missing values; fillna replaces them. The right choice depends on whether a reasonable substitute exists.

blocks.text: `dropna()` removes rows that contain missing values; passing a `subset` of column labels restricts which columns are checked. `fillna()` replaces missing values with a specified value. Drop the row if a missing field makes it unusable for the analysis; fill it if a reasonable substitute — such as the column's median — exists instead.

before.code:
# Missing delivery_time_minutes — two options
print(orders["delivery_time_minutes"].isna().sum())  # count of missing

annotations.text: isna().sum() counts how many values are missing

after.code:
# Drop rows where delivery_time_minutes is missing
orders_dropped = orders.dropna(subset=["delivery_time_minutes"])

# OR fill missing values with the column median
orders["delivery_time_minutes"] = orders["delivery_time_minutes"].fillna(
    orders["delivery_time_minutes"].median()
)

annotations.text: dropna removes rows missing this column
fillna replaces each blank with the median — no rows lost

blocks.change_summary: Missing delivery_time_minutes handled with either dropna (removes rows) or fillna with median (preserves rows).

tiles.title: Descriptive Statistics with pandas
tiles.summary: Compute mean, median, and standard deviation for a DataFrame column, and use describe() to get a full summary in one call.

steps.title: Computing statistics directly from a column
steps.lede: pandas can compute the mean, median, and standard deviation you've calculated by hand — straight from a DataFrame column.

blocks.text: The mean, median, and standard deviation computed by hand earlier for the seven-value delivery-time batch are exactly what pandas can compute directly from a DataFrame column.

pandas provides built-in statistical methods for a Series or DataFrame column, including `mean()` (mean of values), `median()` (arithmetic median), and `std()` (sample standard deviation): if `delivery_time_minutes` holds all fourteen orders, `orders["delivery_time_minutes"].mean()`, `.median()`, and `.std()` return approximately 29.0, 25.0, and 15.6 minutes.

`describe()` computes a set of summary statistics — count, mean, std, min, quartiles, and max — for a Series or for each numeric column of a DataFrame in one call: `orders["delivery_time_minutes"].describe()` returns all of those figures at once for the delivery-time column.

blocks.alt_text: Side-by-side comparison of describe() output and single-method results for delivery_time_minutes. The describe() rows mean=29.0, std=15.6, 50%=25.0 (median), min=18, and max=80 are each connected by arrows to the matching single-method call (.mean(), .std(), .median(), .min(), .max()) showing they return the same value.

For the SwiftDrop delivery-time column, the mean (29.0 min) sits above the median (25.0 min) because a single 80-minute outlier pulls the average up — a pattern describe() makes immediately visible.

remediation_steps.title: Reading the describe() output
remediation_steps.lede: describe() returns a fixed set of rows. Knowing what each row means lets you read any summary table quickly.

blocks.text: `describe()` computes a set of summary statistics — count, mean, std, min, quartiles (25%, 50%, 75%), and max — for a Series or for each numeric column of a DataFrame in one call. The `50%` row is the median. For the SwiftDrop delivery-time column (all fourteen orders), `describe()` shows count 14, mean 29.0, std 15.6, min 18, 25% 21.25, 50% (median) 25.0, 75% 30.25, and max 80.

# count    14.0
# mean     29.0
# std      15.6

steps.title: Replacing values element-by-element with .map()
steps.lede: Every order in the SwiftDrop dataset carries a three-letter city code. .map() lets you swap each code for its full city name in one line.

blocks.text: `Series.map()` accepts a Python function that takes a single value and returns a single value, then applies it to every element of the Series. Define `def to_upper(code): return code.upper()` and call `orders["city_code"].map(to_upper)` — every city code in the column is uppercased in one pass.

`Series.map()` also accepts a **dict** or another **Series** as a mapping correspondence. `orders["city_code"].map({"LOS": "Lagos", "ABJ": "Abuja", "KAN": "Kano"})` replaces each three-letter code with its full city name — no loop, no conditional logic.

before.caption: orders — city_code column holds three-letter codes

annotations.text: Dict maps each code to its full city name
.map(city_lookup) substitutes every code in one call

blocks.change_summary: city_code column (LOS/ABJ/KAN) mapped to full city names (Lagos/Abuja/Kano) using a dict lookup.

steps.title: Running a custom function across rows or columns with .apply()
steps.lede: When you need logic that spans multiple columns — like labelling an order 'fast' or 'slow' based on its delivery time — .apply() runs your function once per row.

blocks.text: Suppose you want to label every SwiftDrop order "fast" or "slow" based on its delivery time, using a rule you write yourself. `Series.map()` works on one column at a time, but this rule needs to read `delivery_time_minutes` and write a new column — that's a row-level operation.

`DataFrame.apply()` applies an arbitrary function along an axis of the DataFrame, operating on each **column** by default (`axis=0`), or on each **row** when `axis=1`. Write `def label_speed(row): return 'slow' if row['delivery_time_minutes'] > 25 else 'fast'`, then `orders.apply(label_speed, axis=1)` runs it once per row and returns one label per order.

blocks.alt_text: A DataFrame feeds into an axis decision: axis=0 runs the function once per column producing one result per column; axis=1 runs it once per row producing one result per row. Both paths collect results into a Series.

steps.title: Map substitution and apply — key takeaways
steps.lede: Two tools for element-wise transformation: .map() for value substitution, .apply() for custom row or column logic.

blocks.text: `Series.map()` substitutes values element-by-element using a function, a dict, or another Series — ideal for recoding categories like city codes. `DataFrame.apply()` runs an arbitrary function along an axis: column-by-column by default, or row-by-row with `axis=1`. Use `apply()` when the logic needs to read across multiple columns of the same row.

remediation_steps.title: How .map() substitutes values — with a function or a dict
remediation_steps.lede: .map() accepts either a Python function or a dict. When you pass a function it is called on every element; when you pass a dict each matching key is replaced by its value.

blocks.text: `Series.map()` accepts a Python function that takes a single value and returns a single value, then applies it to every element of the Series. Define `def to_upper(code): return code.upper()` and call `orders["city_code"].map(to_upper)` — every city code is uppercased in one pass, with no loop.

`Series.map()` also accepts a **dict** as a mapping correspondence. Every element whose value matches a key is replaced by the corresponding dict value; elements with no matching key become `NaN`. Pass `{"LOS": "Lagos", "ABJ": "Abuja", "KAN": "Kano"}` to replace three-letter city codes with full names in one call.

before.code:
# city_code column holds: 'LOS', 'ABJ', 'KAN'
print(orders["city_code"].head(3))
# LOS, ABJ, KAN

annotations.text: Three-letter codes — not human-readable

after.code:
city_lookup = {"LOS": "Lagos", "ABJ": "Abuja", "KAN": "Kano"}
orders["city_name"] = orders["city_code"].map(city_lookup)
print(orders["city_name"].head(3))
# Lagos, Abuja, Kano

annotations.text: Dict: each code → full city name
.map(dict) replaces every code in one call

blocks.change_summary: city_code values (LOS/ABJ/KAN) replaced with full city names (Lagos/Abuja/Kano) via dict lookup.

remediation_steps.title: What axis=1 means for .apply()
remediation_steps.lede: The axis argument tells .apply() which direction to travel — down columns or across rows.

blocks.text: `DataFrame.apply()` applies an arbitrary function along an axis of the DataFrame, operating on each column by default (`axis=0`), or on each row when `axis=1`. With `axis=1`, the function receives one row at a time as a Series, so it can read any column of that row. The return value becomes one element in the result Series — one label per order, for example.

annotations.text: axis=0: function sees each column as a Series

after.code:
# axis=1: function receives one row at a time
def label_speed(row):
    return 'slow' if row['delivery_time_minutes'] > 25 else 'fast'

orders['speed_label'] = orders.apply(label_speed, axis=1)

annotations.text: axis=1: function sees each row — can read any column

blocks.change_summary: axis=0 passes each column to the function; axis=1 passes each row, enabling multi-column logic.

tiles.title: Grouping, Aggregating, and Reshaping with melt

steps.title: Split, apply, combine — groupby in three steps
steps.lede: To find the average delivery time per city, you don't filter and average three times. groupby does all three steps — split, apply, combine — in one call.

blocks.text: **Group by** refers to a process involving one or more of the following steps: splitting the data into groups based on some criteria, applying a function to each group independently, and combining the results into a data structure. For SwiftDrop orders, that means splitting every order into its city's group, applying "average" within each group, then combining the per-city averages into one result.

An **aggregation** is a groupby operation that reduces each group to a single summary value per column — for example, computing the sum of `order_value` within each city group. The result has one row per group, not one row per original order.

blocks.title: Split → Apply → Combine
blocks.alt_text: 8 order rows are split into three city groups (Lagos, Abuja, Kano). An aggregation function is applied inside each group. The per-group results are combined into one summary table with one row per city.

steps.title: groupby in practice
steps.lede: Watch groupby split orders by city and aggregate delivery times and order values.

steps.title: Calling groupby and choosing an aggregation
steps.lede: One call chains the grouping key with the aggregation method. You can compute one statistic or several at once.

blocks.text: Call `df.groupby(key)` then chain an aggregation method such as `.sum()` or `.mean()` on the DataFrame or a selected column. Use `.agg([...])` to compute several aggregations at once. By default, the group keys become the index of the result: `orders.groupby("city")["delivery_time_minutes"].mean()` returns one average per city with city names as the index; `orders.groupby("city")["delivery_time_minutes"].agg(["mean", "sum"])` computes both in one call.

steps.title: Turning a wide table into a long one with melt()
steps.lede: A wide summary table has one column per month. melt() unpivots those columns into rows — one row per city-month combination.

blocks.text: The SwiftDrop monthly deliveries table has one row per city and separate columns `jan_deliveries`, `feb_deliveries`, `mar_deliveries`. Many analysis tools and visualisation libraries expect one row per city-month combination instead — that's the long format.

`melt()` reshapes a DataFrame from wide to long format: the columns listed as `id_vars` stay as identifier columns, while all other columns are unpivoted into two new columns — one holding the original column names and one holding their values. `city_deliveries.melt(id_vars=["city"])` keeps `city` as an identifier and turns the three month columns into two new columns.

The default output column names are `variable` and `value`. Use `var_name` and `value_name` to rename them: `city_deliveries.melt(id_vars=["city"], var_name="month", value_name="deliveries")` gives the two new columns clearer names.

after.caption: Long format — one row per city-month, month column renamed via var_name='month'

blocks.change_summary: Wide table (3 rows × 4 columns) melted to long format (9 rows × 3 columns) with id_vars=['city'], var_name='month', value_name='deliveries'.

steps.title: Groupby aggregation and melt — key takeaways
steps.lede: groupby summarises data by group; melt reshapes wide tables into the long format that analysis tools commonly expect.

blocks.text: Split, apply, combine is the whole idea — `groupby` gives you one call that does all three steps for whatever key and aggregation you choose. Chain `.mean()`, `.sum()`, or `.agg([...])` after `groupby(key)` to get per-group summaries; the group keys become the result's index by default. `melt()` is the complementary reshape: it unpivots wide columns into rows, keeping `id_vars` fixed and turning the rest into a `variable`/`value` pair that you can rename with `var_name` and `value_name`.

remediation_steps.title: The three steps inside every groupby call
remediation_steps.lede: groupby always does the same three things: split the rows into groups, apply a function to each group, then combine the results.

blocks.text: **Group by** refers to a process involving one or more of the following steps: splitting the data into groups based on some criteria, applying a function to each group independently, and combining the results into a data structure. For SwiftDrop orders: split every order into its city's group, apply "average delivery time" within each group, then combine the per-city averages into one summary table.

remediation_steps.title: Renaming the variable and value columns in melt()
remediation_steps.lede: melt() always produces two new columns. By default they're called 'variable' and 'value' — var_name and value_name let you rename them.

blocks.text: The default `variable` and `value` column names produced by `melt()` can be renamed using its `var_name` and `value_name` parameters. Passing `var_name="month"` renames the column that holds the original column names; passing `value_name="deliveries"` renames the column that holds their values.

before.code:
# Without renaming — default column names
city_deliveries.melt(id_vars=['city'])
# Columns: city | variable | value

annotations.text: Default names 'variable' and 'value' are generic

after.code:
# With var_name and value_name
city_deliveries.melt(
    id_vars=['city'],
    var_name='month',
    value_name='deliveries'
)
# Columns: city | month | deliveries

steps.title: Stacking DataFrames with pd.concat()
steps.lede: January, February, and March orders each live in their own table. pd.concat() glues them into one combined DataFrame in a single call.

blocks.text: `pd.concat()` concatenates multiple Series or DataFrame objects along an axis. Pass a list of DataFrames: `pd.concat([jan_orders, feb_orders, mar_orders])`. By default it stacks them **row-wise**, appending each one's rows below the previous — so the result has every January row, then every February row, then every March row, one after another.

`pd.concat()` takes an `axis` parameter. By default (no `axis` argument) it stacks row-wise. Passing `axis=1` places the DataFrames side by side as columns: `pd.concat([orders_basic_info, orders_extra_columns], axis=1)` lines the two tables up next to each other, column by column.

all_orders = pd.concat([jan_orders, feb_orders, mar_orders])
print(all_orders.shape)  # (15, 5)
print(all_orders.head())

15 rows = 5 Jan + 5 Feb + 5 Mar

steps.title: Joining two DataFrames on a shared key with merge()
steps.lede: Orders and driver details live in separate tables, linked by driver_id. merge() matches rows on that shared key and combines the columns.

blocks.text: `merge()` combines two DataFrames by matching values in a shared key column, specified with the `on` parameter: `orders.merge(drivers, on="driver_id")`. The result contains one row for every matched pair — columns from both tables side by side.

The `how` parameter controls which keys are kept. `how='inner'` (the default) keeps only key values present in **both** DataFrames — a `driver_id` that appears in orders but not in drivers won't survive an inner merge, and vice versa.

When a key value does not appear in one of the two DataFrames, the corresponding values contributed by that DataFrame in the joined result are `NA`. This is what happens once a join type other than the default inner merge is used and unmatched keys are allowed to stay in the result.

steps.title: Left, right, and outer joins
steps.lede: Beyond the default inner join, three other how= values let you keep unmatched rows from one or both sides.

blocks.text: The `how` parameter also accepts `'left'` (keep all keys from the left DataFrame only), `'right'` (keep all keys from the right DataFrame only), and `'outer'` (keep the union of keys from both DataFrames). `orders.merge(drivers, on="driver_id", how="left")` keeps every order, filling in `NA` for driver details on any `driver_id` that merge can't find in the drivers table.

steps.title: Concatenation and merging — key takeaways
steps.lede: concat glues tables end to end; merge matches rows on a shared key. The axis and how parameters control the direction and which rows survive.

blocks.text: `pd.concat()` glues tables end to end — the `axis` argument is just which direction: down for more rows (default), sideways for more columns. `merge()` matches rows on a shared key; setting `how` decides whether unmatched rows on either side get dropped (`inner`) or kept with `NA` gaps (`left`, `right`, `outer`). Use concat when tables share the same columns; use merge when they share a key column.

blocks.text: `merge()` combines two DataFrames by matching values in a shared key column specified with `on`. The `how` parameter controls which keys are kept: `how='inner'` (the default) keeps only key values present in both DataFrames. `how='left'` keeps all keys from the left DataFrame, filling `NA` for any driver details that can't be found in the right table.

remediation_steps.title: Why unmatched keys produce NA values
remediation_steps.lede: When a key value exists on only one side of a merge, the columns from the missing side have nothing to contribute — so they become NA.

blocks.text: If a key value does not appear in one of the two DataFrames being merged, the corresponding values contributed by that DataFrame in the joined result are `NA`. This is what happens once a join type other than the default inner merge is used and unmatched keys are allowed to stay in the result — for example, a `driver_id` that exists in orders but not in drivers will have `NA` in every driver column.

tiles.title: Pivot Tables and Exporting to CSV

steps.title: Spreading long data into a wide grid with pivot_table()
steps.lede: The long deliveries table has one row per city-month. pivot_table() spreads it back into a wide grid — cities as rows, months as columns — and handles duplicate cells automatically.

blocks.text: `pivot_table()` reshapes data by turning the distinct values of one column into new columns. Unlike plain `pivot()`, it can handle duplicate index/column combinations by aggregating the numeric values — so it won't raise an error if two rows share the same city and month.

`pivot_table()` takes `index`, `columns`, and `values` arguments: `index` sets the rows of the output table, `columns` sets the new columns, and `values` selects which column to aggregate. `long_deliveries.pivot_table(index="city", columns="month", values="deliveries")` puts each city on its own row, each month as its own column, and the delivery counts as the values filling the grid.

before.caption: long_deliveries — one row per city-month combination

after.code:
wide = long_deliveries.pivot_table(
    index='city',
    columns='month',
    values='deliveries'
)
print(wide)

annotations.text: index='city' → cities become rows
columns='month' → month values become column headers
values='deliveries' → delivery counts fill the grid

blocks.change_summary: Long table (8 rows × 3 columns) pivoted to wide format (3 rows × 3 month columns) with city as index.

steps.title: Controlling how duplicate cells are combined with aggfunc
steps.lede: When two rows share the same index and column values, pivot_table() must combine them. aggfunc controls how.

blocks.text: `pivot_table()` combines rows that share the same index/column values using `aggfunc`, which defaults to `'mean'`. Passing `aggfunc='sum'` (or another function) changes how those values are combined — so if a city had two rows for the same month, the default call would average them instead of erroring, and adding `aggfunc='sum'` would total them instead.

steps.title: Writing a DataFrame to a CSV file with to_csv()
steps.lede: Once the data is clean and shaped, to_csv() writes it to a file. One argument controls whether the row index is included.

blocks.text: The `to_csv()` method on a Series or DataFrame writes its contents to a CSV file; the destination path or buffer is its only required argument: `orders.to_csv("cleaned_orders.csv")` writes the full orders table to a file.

`to_csv()`'s `index` argument controls whether the row labels are written to the file; it defaults to `True`. Passing `index=False` omits them: `orders.to_csv("cleaned_orders.csv", index=False)` writes the same file without an extra index column at the start.

# 0,1001,Lagos,18,...
# 1,1002,Abuja,20,...

annotations.text: Leading comma = unnamed index column written to file

right.code:
orders.to_csv('cleaned_orders.csv', index=False)
# CSV has no extra column:
# order_id,city,delivery_time_minutes,...
# 1001,Lagos,18,...
# 1002,Abuja,20,...

annotations.text: No leading comma — index omitted from file

blocks.takeaway: Pass index=False whenever the row index is just a default integer range and you don't want it as a column in the output file.

remediation_steps.title: How aggfunc controls duplicate cell values in pivot_table()
remediation_steps.lede: When two rows share the same index and column values, pivot_table() must combine them. aggfunc tells it how.

blocks.text: `pivot_table()` combines rows that share the same index/column values using `aggfunc`, which defaults to `'mean'`. Passing `aggfunc='sum'` changes how those values are combined — so if a city had two rows for the same month, the default call would average them instead of erroring, and adding `aggfunc='sum'` would total them instead.

before.code:
# Default aggfunc='mean'
wide = long_deliveries.pivot_table(
    index='city', columns='month', values='deliveries'
)
# Duplicate city-month rows are averaged

annotations.text: aggfunc='mean' is the default — duplicates averaged

after.code:
# aggfunc='sum' totals duplicate rows instead
wide = long_deliveries.pivot_table(
    index='city', columns='month', values='deliveries',
    aggfunc='sum'
)
# Duplicate city-month rows are summed

annotations.text: aggfunc='sum' → duplicates totalled, not averaged

blocks.change_summary: Default aggfunc='mean' averages duplicate cells; aggfunc='sum' totals them instead.

remediation_steps.title: The index argument in to_csv()
remediation_steps.lede: By default to_csv() writes the row index as an extra column. index=False omits it.

blocks.text: `to_csv()`'s `index` argument controls whether the row (index) labels are written to the file; it defaults to `True`, and passing `index=False` omits them. When the index is just a default integer range (0, 1, 2, …), it adds an unnamed column to the CSV that most downstream tools don't expect — `index=False` prevents that.

before.code:
# index=True (default) — row labels written to file
orders.to_csv('cleaned_orders.csv')
# First column in file: 0, 1, 2, ... (the index)

annotations.text: Extra unnamed column — the DataFrame's row index

after.code:
# index=False — row labels omitted
orders.to_csv('cleaned_orders.csv', index=False)
# File starts directly with order_id, city, ...

annotations.text: No extra column — cleaner output for downstream tools

blocks.change_summary: index=True (default) writes row labels as an extra column; index=False omits them.
